comments.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

The reranker finding is the one I would put first rather than third, because it is the one that contradicts the strongest prior.

"Add a reranker" is close to universal advice, and the measurement here shows it making retrieval *worse at every k* on this corpus. What makes it a good finding is not that reranking is bad — it is that the proxy cross-encoder is fitted on features that the first stage has already optimised for, so it reorders without adding information.

**The transferable version:** a reranker only helps if it can see something the first stage could not. A reranker over the same signals as the retriever is an expensive identity function, and occasionally worse than one.

replies.body:
That is a better statement of it than the one in the post, and I am going to lift it into the README's finding.

The measurement that would change the conclusion is a genuine cross-encoder doing full attention over the query-document pair — that *does* see something the bi-encoder cannot. [#15](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/issues/15) is open for exactly this and is a good second issue for someone.

comments.body:
> **Noor** · cohort peer · works in a regulated bank

What makes this page unusual is keeping the findings that contradict the teaching material rather than quietly re-running until they agreed.

Would suggest one addition: for each finding, a line saying **what would change the conclusion.** "This is true on this corpus with this encoder" is much stronger with "and here is the experiment that would overturn it" attached — it is the difference between a result and a claim.

replies.body: Agreed and adopting it. Adding a *"what would change this"* line to all three findings, and to the ADR template — [`docs/adr/template.md`](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/blob/main/docs/adr/template.md) currently has "consequences" but nothing that names the falsifier.
